prompt: Why does an iOS app usually drop support for old system versions sooner than an Android app?

choices.text: Android phones are updated by Google directly, so they are newer

prompt: A user installs a study app, uses it daily for a month, then stops opening it for two weeks on an Android 14 phone. What should the app's developer expect for its background jobs?

choices.text: Nothing changes: a month of daily use keeps it in the active bucket
choices.why: Buckets follow recent use; two weeks without opening it moves it down.

choices.text: Its jobs run more often, to win the user back
choices.why: Less use means more restriction, never less.

choices.text: The app is uninstalled automatically
choices.why: The system restricts the app; it does not remove it.

choices.text: Expect them to run once a day, batched with other apps
choices.why: Right. Past 8 days unopened, the restricted bucket allows one batched session a day.

prompt: When an Android phone lies unplugged, still and with its screen off, it enters a state called ___, which defers jobs and cuts network access.
A podcast app keeps downloaded episodes it can fetch again, and the listener's subscriptions, which it cannot. Where does each go on iOS?

choices.text: Both in Documents
choices.why: Episodes in Documents fill the user's backup with files the app could fetch again.

choices.text: Both in tmp
choices.why: tmp is purged when the app is not running.

choices.text: Episodes in Library/Caches, subscriptions in Application Support
choices.why: Right. What can be fetched again may be purged; what cannot is kept and backed up.

choices.text: Subscriptions in Library/Caches, episodes in Application Support
choices.why: The other way round: the subscriptions are the ones that cannot be rebuilt.

prompt: Which of these belong in the Keychain or the Keystore rather than in preferences? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A refresh token that renews the user's session
choices.why: Right. Whoever holds it can act as the user.

choices.text: The password for the user's account
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether the user prefers the dark theme
choices.why: A preference, and harmless to read.

choices.text: The last tab the user had open
choices.why: A preference; losing it costs one tap.

prompt: An app writes its settings with writeFileSync straight over settings.json. Users report, rarely, that all their settings reset after the phone died. Which change fixes it?

choices.text: Write a temporary file, then rename it
choices.why: Right. A half-written file no longer parses and the app falls back to defaults; a rename is never half-done.

choices.text: Move settings.json to the cache
choices.why: That adds a second way to lose it.

choices.text: Write the file twice
choices.why: Two in-place writes have two moments to be cut short.

choices.text: Catch the parse error and show it to the user
choices.why: That reports the loss without preventing it.

prompt: An Android app has 31 MB of data that Auto Backup would include. How many megabytes over the per-app limit is it?

A messaging app stores each user's device token once, at sign-up, and never updates it. Some users report that notifications stopped after they changed phones. Why?

choices.text: The new phone blocks notifications from apps restored from a backup
choices.why: Nothing blocks them; they are addressed to the wrong place.

choices.text: The push service only delivers to the phone used at sign-up
choices.why: It delivers to whatever token it is given.

choices.text: Tokens expire after a fixed number of messages
choices.why: They change on events such as a new device, not on a count.

choices.text: A new phone means a new token; the server still holds the old one
choices.why: Right. The app should send its token at every launch, and the server keep it current.

prompt: A message's JSON measures 3,900 bytes and the developer wants to add a field of 250 bytes. By how many bytes would it exceed a 4096-byte limit?
A medication app must remind a patient at 08:00 every day, including on days with no network. Which mechanism fits?

choices.text: A push from the server at 08:00
choices.why: With no network it cannot arrive, and a push is best effort anyway.

choices.text: A local notification the system schedules
choices.why: Right. The phone keeps the appointment with no server and no network.

choices.text: A periodic background job every 24 hours
choices.why: The system chooses when it runs; 08:00 is not a promise it makes.

choices.text: A data-only push that wakes the app
choices.why: It needs the network, and its delivery to the app is not guaranteed.

choices.text: The corner where the add button sits
choices.why: Each guide has its own place for the main action.

choices.text: The font used for body text

choices.text: The name and shape of the bar of sections

prompt: An Android app wants its brand's own green on every phone, including on Android 12 and later. What does it do about dynamic colour?

choices.why: The system offers a scheme; the app decides whether to use it.

choices.text: Sets its minimum version below Android 12

choices.text: Uses a wallpaper that is the brand's green

prompt: An icon-only button in an app declares no label. What does a screen reader user hear when focus reaches it?

choices.why: Screen readers read declarations, not pixels.

choices.text: The app's name
choices.why: The app's name is not a fallback for a control's label.

choices.text: Nothing: elements without a label are skipped

choices.text: Nothing grows; use a text style and let the row's height follow

choices.text: The row clips its text; raise the fixed height to 60
